name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
summary: Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel causing nocturnal paresthesia, sensory symptoms and sometimes thenar weakness.

looksLike: Numbness/tingling thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger
firstSteps: Neutral wrist night splint when appropriate

tests.name: Phalen Test
tests.purpose: Provoke median nerve symptoms by sustained wrist flexion.

tests.name: Durkan Carpal Compression Test
tests.purpose: Directly increase pressure over the carpal tunnel.

tests.name: Tinel Sign at Wrist
tests.purpose: Assess irritability of median nerve at carpal tunnel.

stages.label: Reduce Compression & Night Symptoms
stages.goal: Reduce sustained wrist compression and improve sleep.
do: Neutral wrist night splint when appropriate
dose: Gentle tendon/nerve gliding: 1–3 sets of 5–10, avoiding symptom flare

stages.label: Function & Contributing Factors
stages.goal: Restore hand/forearm capacity without provoking nerve symptoms.
moveOn: Functional tasks tolerated with less paresthesia

logic: Mild-to-moderate cases may respond to night splinting, activity modification and nerve/tendon gliding.
Progressive thenar weakness or constant major sensory loss needs medical review.
classification: Severe with weakness/thenar atrophy or marked electrodiagnostic change
investigations: Electrodiagnostic testing is useful for severity, atypical cases and preoperative evaluation depending on guideline/pathway.
Ultrasound may be used in selected settings.
manual: Neural/tendon gliding and selected carpal mobilization may be used as adjuncts.
Avoid aggressive nerve stretching that reproduces persistent paresthesia.
Carpal/forearm soft-tissue or joint techniques as adjuncts when they improve symptoms
Median nerve sliders should remain gentle and should not create prolonged numbness.
Carpal/forearm mobilization can be trialed if it improves symptoms.
Avoid aggressive pressure directly over the carpal tunnel.
modalities: Night splinting is more clinically relevant than routine electrotherapy.
Escalate for medical/surgical review when weakness, thenar atrophy or persistent significant symptoms occur.
Neutral wrist splint at night is commonly useful
Electrotherapy is not a core long-term treatment
Night neutral wrist splinting is often more useful than electrotherapy for symptom control.
dosing: Median nerve slider: 5–10 gentle reps, 1–3 times/day initially.
progression: Increase hand loading as paresthesia and irritability improve
Increase hand loading as nocturnal symptoms and irritability reduce.
mistakes: Delaying referral when motor loss appears
Keeping the wrist splint on all day without need.
pearls: Nocturnal median-distribution paresthesia is a classic history clue.
Provocative tests support but do not replace a full neurologic and upper-quarter examination.
education: Avoid long sustained wrist flexion/extension when possible.
Use frequent micro-breaks for repetitive work.
Explain when surgical/medical opinion may be needed.
escalation: Medical/hand-surgery review for progressive weakness, atrophy or persistent significant sensory loss

tests.name: Phalen Test
tests.purpose: Provoke median nerve symptoms by sustained wrist flexion.
tests.handPlacement: Patient places dorsal hands together with wrists maximally flexed as tolerated.
procedure: Flex both wrists and press backs of hands together.
Hold up to about 60 seconds or until symptoms occur.
tests.interpretation: Supports CTS; should be combined with history and other examination findings.

tests.name: Durkan Carpal Compression Test
tests.purpose: Directly increase pressure over the carpal tunnel.
tests.handPlacement: Thumbs/fingers over the carpal tunnel just distal to wrist crease.
procedure: Apply firm direct pressure over carpal tunnel.
Maintain for up to about 30 seconds or until symptoms reproduce.

tests.name: Tinel Sign at Wrist
tests.purpose: Assess irritability of median nerve at carpal tunnel.
tests.handPlacement: Tap gently over median nerve/carpal tunnel.
procedure: Percuss over the carpal tunnel several times.
Ask whether tingling radiates into median-innervated digits.

story.headline: The midnight hand alarm and the nerve with a narrow hallway
story.scene: A graphic designer wakes at 2 a.m. shaking a tingling hand. The thumb, index and middle fingers complain most. The little finger seems suspiciously quiet.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Maybe my whole arm has fallen asleep?' Therapist: 'Let's ask which fingers attended the meeting.'
story.clue: Night symptoms and median-distribution paresthesia support carpal tunnel syndrome. The little finger is usually spared, but symptom patterns vary and proximal causes remain possible.
story.twist: A provocative test on its own does not settle the diagnosis. Constant numbness or progressive thenar weakness warrants timely further assessment.
story.aha: The quiet little finger is a clue, not a magic rule.
story.patientTranslation: A nerve at the wrist may be under pressure and causing the night-time tingling. Simple strategies, such as a neutral night splint for suitable cases, may help; worsening weakness needs assessment.
story.clinicianReasoning: Map sensory distribution; examine thenar strength and atrophy, proximal neural contributors and systemic neuropathy risk. Use history and examination with electrodiagnostics when indicated; consider referral for progressive deficits.
story.rehabBridge: Reduce aggravating wrist positions and nighttime symptoms → optimize function and ergonomic load → reassess sensation/strength and refer when indicated.
story.question: Which symptom cluster most supports carpal tunnel syndrome?
story.explanation: Nocturnal median-distribution paresthesia is a classic CTS presentation, but assessment should exclude other causes.
